281.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
281.explanation: In a salok of the Vaar in Raag Maajh, Guru Nanak takes what each community holds most forbidden and says that taking another's due is just as forbidden. Sikh teaching sets this beside kirat karni, earning by honest work.
281.tie_back: The Kural tells anyone who wants to avoid contempt to guard against taking anything of another's by stealth. Guru Nanak's comparison makes such taking the deepest kind of defilement.
281.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
281._accuracy_note: A strong and direct match on not taking what belongs to another. The Kural's reason is avoiding contempt, while Guru Nanak's is defilement before God.

282.quote_or_event: “False is the mind which covets the wealth of others.”
282.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan names each faculty that goes astray: the hands that steal, the ears that slander, and here the mind that covets another's wealth.
282.tie_back: The Kural finds wrong in merely thinking of taking another's property by cunning. Guru Arjan likewise condemns the coveting mind itself, before any act.
282.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 269, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
282._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match: both place the fault in the mind's desire for another's goods. Gurbani speaks of coveting in general, not specifically of plotting fraud.

283.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
283.explanation: In one of the Babar hymns in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak reflects on the wealth of rulers ruined by invasion. It was piled up through wrongdoing, and it could not save them or go with them.
283.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by fraud seems to grow but will perish. Guru Nanak describes wealth gained through sin that cannot last and abandons its owner at death.
283.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
283._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on ill-gotten wealth that does not last. The hymn's setting is the ruin of rulers in Babar's invasion, not private fraud.

284.quote_or_event: “Those who are attached to the poison of greed and sin grab at the wealth of others; they only bring pain on themselves.”
284.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan says that people held by greed seize others' wealth and harvest only suffering. Sikh teaching names greed (lobh) as one of the five thieves within.
284.tie_back: The Kural warns that a hardened craving for gain by fraud bears fruit in endless sorrow. Guru Arjan likewise traces the grabbing of others' wealth to greed and says it ends in pain for the grabber.
284.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 408, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
284._accuracy_note: A strong fit: craving leads to taking others' wealth, which leads to the taker's own suffering. Gurbani does not stress the Kural's point that the sorrow is unending.

285.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
285.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak sang this hymn at the inn of Sajjan. Sajjan seemed a pious host to travellers but robbed them once they were off guard, and he repented on hearing it.
285.tie_back: The Kural says those who covet others' goods and wait for a moment of carelessness cannot have loving compassion. Sajjan's polished hospitality hiding a predator's watchfulness is exactly that bright surface over darkness.
285.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
285._accuracy_note: The quote is verified scripture, but its link to the robber Sajjan is Janamsakhi hagiography. The verse itself speaks of false appearances in general, not of watching for another's lapse.

286.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan describes a person who heaps up Maya and pleasures but never feels satisfied. He wears himself out chasing more, and only contentment (santokh) brings rest.
286.tie_back: The Kural says those hardened in love of fraudulent gain cannot keep within measure. Guru Arjan names contentment as the missing measure, without which desire knows no limit.
286.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
286._accuracy_note: A strong fit if aḷavu is read, as Mu. Varadarasan does, as contentment or limit. Gurbani does not tie the lack of contentment specifically to fraud.

287.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end.”
287.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak dismisses cleverness (siaanap) as a way to reach truth. Only walking in the Hukam, God's order, removes the wall of falsehood.
287.tie_back: The Kural calls fraud a 'dark cleverness' that is absent in those who have chosen the strength of measure. Japji likewise sets worldly cunning against the true discipline it can never replace.
287.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
287._accuracy_note: Next-best: both reject calculating cleverness. Japji opposes it to God's Hukam rather than to the virtue of measure or restraint, and it does not speak of fraud.

288.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
288.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid contrasts those whose love is true in the heart with those whose inner mind and outward words do not match.
288.tie_back: The Kural says virtue abides in the hearts of those who know measure, while deceit abides in the hearts of those who have learned fraud. Farid likewise judges people by what is settled in the heart, not by what they show.
288.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
288._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on deceit as a settled condition of the heart. Farid's subject is false love of God, not habitual fraud, and the verse is by a Bhagat included in the Granth, not by a Guru.

289.quote_or_event: “O my mind, do not practice deception, even inadvertently. In the end, your own soul shall have to answer for its account.”
289.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir describes a man who brings home others' wealth through many deceptions. He warns that the deceiver's own soul must render the account, and none of those he fed will help him.
289.tie_back: The Kural says those who know no way of living but fraud are destroyed by their own measureless deeds. Kabir likewise makes the deceiver's ruin the direct reckoning of his own deception.
289.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
289._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on a life built on deception that ends in self-ruin. Kabir places the reckoning at the end of life, while the Kural stresses ruin in the act itself.

290.quote_or_event: “One who does not steal the wealth of others, who does not commit evil deeds or sinful acts - the Messenger of Death does not even approach him.”
290.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan says that one who sings God's praises and keeps clear of others' wealth is beyond the reach of Death's messenger.
290.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying the world of the gods will not fail those who never defraud. Guru Arjan likewise promises that one who never takes others' wealth is safe from Death's messenger.
290.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
290._accuracy_note: A strong match for the Kural's second half. Gurbani promises freedom from Death's messenger rather than a heaven of the gods, and it says nothing explicit about the defrauder's life failing him.
